paragraphs: Muttar litten betza bachamma beshabbat shettitztzaleh, mippene sheen derek bishshul bekak. veken muttar litten mayim bachamma kede sheyyeyachamu. vehambashshel beor beshabbat chayyab, veim asa bemezid, asur lo leolam, vegam haqqedera asura lo belo hagala, mippene shebbelua meissur utzerika heksher kishar kelim habbeluim meissur; velaacherim muttar lemotzae-shabbat miyyad. veim beshogeg, asur bo bayyom - ben lo, ben laacherim – ulemotzae-shabbat muttar miyyad - ben lo, ben laacherim. veim hannakeri bishshel dabar sheen bo bishshule goyim, o sheasa shear melaka leyisrael, asur bo bayyom, ulemotzae-shabbat yamtin bikde sheyyeasu, degazeru bimlaka shel nakeri tepe, dechashu pen yomar yisrael lenakeri laasot lo melaka beshabbat kede sheyyehaneh mimmenna bemotzae-shabbat miyyad, ki issur amira lenakeri beshabbat qal beene adam.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to place an egg in the sun (sunlight) on the Sabbath so that it roasts, and likewise to place water in the sun so it warms — since this is not considered a normal "manner of cooking," and so there is no prohibition in it. By contrast, one who actually cooks over fire on the Sabbath transgresses a severe prohibition. If he did so deliberately (intentionally), he may never benefit from the dish, and the pot itself is forbidden for use until it is koshered by hagalah (purging), since it is "absorbed" with a forbidden substance. Others (who did not cook) may use the dish immediately at the Sabbath's conclusion. If he cooked unintentionally (by mistake, not knowing it was forbidden), the dish is forbidden only on that Sabbath day itself — both to him and to others — but at the Sabbath's conclusion it is immediately permitted to all. And if a gentile cooked for a Jew something that has no prohibition of "gentile cooking," or performed some other labor for him, the matter is forbidden on the Sabbath itself, and at its conclusion one must wait a period equal to the time it took to perform the labor — since here the Sages were stricter, out of concern that a Jew might ask a gentile to perform labor for him on the Sabbath in order to benefit from it immediately at its conclusion, since the prohibition of telling a gentile is regarded by people as a lighter prohibition.
takeaways: Roasting an egg or warming water in the sun (not fire) is permitted on the Sabbath.
Cooking over fire on the Sabbath deliberately forbids the dish to the cook forever and requires purging the pot; unintentionally, it is forbidden only that day.
A gentile's labor for a Jew's benefit on the Sabbath requires waiting, at its conclusion, an amount of time equal to how long the labor took.

paragraphs: Hambashshel beshabbat bemezid, o sheasa shear melakot bemezid, deamerinan asur lambashshel leolam, umuttar laacherim bemotzae shabbat miyyad - katab mvr"m behaggahat hashshulchan, beyoreh dea, sop siman q"b, deim nitareb hare zeh mitbattel, vela amerinan dachashib "dabar sheyyesh lo mattirim" velo batel mishshum demuttar laacherim achar shabbat, ella kevan delazeh asur leolam, la chashib dabar sheyyesh lo mattirin umitbattel. vekatab haggaon "kereti upeleti" za"l sham, dezeh davqa lambashshel, abal laacherim, apillu im nitbattel eno batel, dachashib ledidehu dabar sheyyesh lo mattirin, veken katab chavvot daat za"l sham, dekavvanat harama" za"l ken hu. veayyen mah shekkatab besipte daat sham. mihu, haggaon magen abraham kan besiman shy"ch, seip qatan b' katab, degam limbashshel asur bo bayyom gam im nitbattel. vaayin laacharonim mah sheppilpelu bedin zeh haka vehatam beyoreh dea, yeuyyan sham. vehinneh ana abeda hebeti din bsh"q "rab-pealim", vekatabti bs"d, shezzeh inyan hu domeh bedomeh liplugetta dipri chadash za"l im rabbane ashkenaz bemaaseh haqqatztzab sheshshachat sheba behemot bebeto veku', kannizkar beseper "bet-hillel", yoreh dea, siman q"y, uperi chadash baqqunetres acharon, yeuyyan sham. veayyen lehaggaon tosepet shabbat bequnteres "bekor shoro", bechiddushe chullin, shehebi pelugta hannizkeret umah shekkatab, ayyen sham. veim ken, banniddon didan - lisbarat haggeonim deaseru hashsheni chatzain, shebbachanut veshebbebet, mishshum dela leheve tarte desatere - gam kan tzarik lehorot kemo sheppasaq magen abraham za"l leesor gam lambashshel benitbattel bo bayyom, abal lipri chadash udeima, yesh lehorot kisbarat mvr"m za"l delaacherim asur benitbattel, velambashshel muttar. veachar asher pilpalti beinyan zeh sham bs"d, heeleti dahalaka - dibniddon didan gam happeri chadash udeima yodu deaserinan benitbattel gam ledideh, mishshum demecheze kechuka tepe umilleta ditmiha: ek lemi sheasa haissur yihyeh muttar, velaacherim yihyeh asur?! veod katabti sham mah sheameru bizbachim, dap s"g dela yihyeh tapel chamur min haiqqar; venireh sham sheddabar zeh muskam lahalaka; veken kan, im laacherim asur velambashshel muttar, nimtza tapel chamur min haiqqar. veod hebeti sham mah shekkatab harab peri chadash besiman qy, besop ot g' vezeh leshono: hane mille, heka dela minnakra milleta, kegon sapeq yemama sapeq layla, abal bemidi deiteh qamman, mechazu mille derabbanan ki chuka veitlula vela sharenan, kidita bepereq ketzad mebarekin ubesop pereq haddar, ad kan leshono ayyen sham. velaken rauy lehorot kemo shekkatab hammagen abraham leesor gam benitbattel, gam ledideh, vehaynu kevateh vela mittameh.

clarification.explanation: This law concerns a case where a person cooked on the Sabbath deliberately (intentionally), so that the dish becomes forever forbidden to him while permitted immediately to others at the Sabbath's conclusion. The question discussed: what happens if such a dish becomes mixed into another dish? Some say (the Rema) that the mixture is nullified by the majority (i.e. the forbidden dish is "nullified" and permitted to all), since this is not a case of "a thing that has permitters" (which is never nullified) — for even to the one who cooked it himself it is forbidden forever and not merely temporarily. Others (Kereti uPeleti) distinguished: regarding one to whom the dish is forbidden only temporarily (until the Sabbath's conclusion), it indeed is not nullified, but to one to whom it is forbidden forever, it is nullified. There is yet another opinion (the Magen Avraham) that even for the cook himself there is no nullification, and it remains forbidden. Rabbi Yosef Chaim (in Rav Pe'alim) discussed this question and compared it to a similar case in the laws of ritual slaughter, ultimately ruling that in this matter one should be stringent even according to the authorities who are generally lenient, for the reason that it seems absurd and contrary to reason that specifically the one who committed the prohibition would be permitted, while others who did nothing wrong would be forbidden — and this also contradicts the principle that the "secondary" matter should not be more severe than the "primary" one.
takeaways: A complex technical ruling on the nullification of a mixture containing a dish cooked in deliberate violation on the Sabbath.
The practical conclusion: one should be stringent and forbid it even to the one who cooked the dish himself, even if it became a minority in the mixture, and not be lenient as some authorities hold.

paragraphs: Ap al gab deamerinan: muttar litzlot betza bachamma, eno ella bachamma atzmah, abal betoledot chamma, kegon sudar shehucham bachamma, asur leshabber habbetza alayv kede litzlotah meat, gezera mishshum toledot haur, sheharoeh chosheb - hucham beor. veken asur legalgelah al hachol vaabaq derakim shehuchammu bekocha chamma.

clarification.explanation: Although it is permitted to roast an egg directly in the sun itself, this is permitted only in the sun's own heat. But if the sun warmed some other object (such as a garment or scarf) and one then wishes to crack an egg onto it to roast it somewhat — this is forbidden. The reason: the Sages decreed against "products of the sun" (something warmed by the sun) out of concern that an onlooker would think the warming was done by fire rather than by the sun. For the same reason, it is also forbidden to roll an egg on sand or road dust that has become hot from the sun's force.
takeaways: The leniency to roast in the sun applies only to the sun itself directly, not to things warmed by it ("products of the sun") such as hot sand or hot cloth.

paragraphs: Hambashshel o asa shear melakot lecholeh sheyyesh bo sakkana, asur beshabbat lebari o lecholeh sheen bo sakkana, leekol mimmennu, gezera shemma yarbeh bimlakto bishbil habbari; abal lemotzae-shabbat muttar lebari miyyad. veken im naasa "y nakeri melaka - ben letzorek choleh sheyyesh bo sakkana, ben lecholeh sheen bo sakkana - asur lebari beshabbat, shemma yarbeh bishbilo, abal lemotzae-shabbat muttar lebari miyyad, veen tzorek lehamtin bikde sheyyeasu. veraq im hayeta hammelaka bebishshul sheyyesh bo issur bishshule goyim, asur lebari leolam mishshum bishshule goyim, vegam lacholeh atzmo achar shabbat, kol sheepshar lebashshel lo mechadash "y yisrael - dela huttar bishshule goyim lecholeh ella raq beshabbat, dei epshar lebashshel lo "y yisrael. veken hakkelim shebbishshel bahem haggoy beshabbat tabshil sheyyesh bo issur bishshule goyim, gam ken asurim achar hashshabbat utzerikin hagala; ukele cheres, magilan shelosh peamim vedayyo, ap al gab dibissurin dealema lo mehanne hagala likli cheres apillu beshalosh peamim - beha mehanne. ubediabad im bishshel bekelim ellu belo heksher veyesh rob tabshil, muttar. veayyen "chayye-adam", kelal s"t, seip t' usheare acharonim, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: One who cooked or performed other labor on the Sabbath for a critically ill patient (which was permitted in order to save him), a healthy person, and even a patient who is not critically ill, may not eat from this food on that same Sabbath — since there is concern they might increase the labor performed for their sake. But at the Sabbath's conclusion, a healthy person may eat immediately. The same applies if a gentile performed the labor for the patient — whether critically ill or not — a healthy person may not benefit from it on the Sabbath, but at the Sabbath's conclusion he may do so immediately without waiting (unlike halacha 1, since here the labor was not performed for the sake of the healthy Jew himself). An exception: if the labor was cooking by a gentile involving the prohibition of "gentile cooking," then the food is forever forbidden to a healthy person, and even to the patient himself after the Sabbath — as long as it is possible to cook it again through a Jew, since the leniency of gentile cooking for a patient applies only on the Sabbath itself (when there is no other option). Vessels in which a gentile cooked a forbidden dish on the Sabbath due to the prohibition of gentile cooking likewise require purging (hagalah) after the Sabbath; if they are earthenware vessels, purging them three times suffices (even though purging generally does not help earthenware vessels at all). After the fact, if food was already cooked in these vessels without koshering and the majority of the dish is kosher, the dish is permitted.
takeaways: Food cooked on the Sabbath for a critically ill patient is forbidden to a healthy person on the Sabbath itself but permitted immediately at its conclusion.
If it involved the prohibition of gentile cooking, it remains forever forbidden to both the healthy person and the patient, unless it cannot be recooked in a kosher manner.

paragraphs: Kol dabar shello nitbashshel qodem shabbat, en shorin oto beshabbat bechammin shehayyad soledet bo, apillu eno nimmocha bishriyya zo. vedin chammin shehayyad soledet bo en meshaarin beetzba, ella kol shekkereso shel tinoq nikvet bahem chashib yad soledet bo. veim tomar, ek yeda haadam leshaer bekak middato? hinneh, naqet hay kelala bidak: kol heka shezzeh hachammin rauy lishtiyya o laakila, sheen haadam nimna mikkoach ribbuy chamimuto, hare zeh la chashib yad soledet bo; veim yimmana millishtoto o leakelo merob chummo, hare zeh nechshab biklal yad soledet bo.

clarification.explanation: A food item that was not cooked at all before the Sabbath may not be soaked on the Sabbath in water hot enough that "a hand recoils from it" (yad soledet bo, meaning a heat so high that a hand pulls back from it), even if this soaking will not cause it to disintegrate. The halachic definition of "a hand recoils from it" is not measured by the finger's sensation, but by the degree at which an infant's stomach would be burned by that heat. How can an ordinary person know this for himself? The practical rule: if the beverage is still fit for drinking or eating, and a person would not avoid it because of the heat, this is not considered "a hand recoils from it." But if a person would avoid drinking or eating it because it is too hot — this is considered "a hand recoils from it," and it is forbidden.
takeaways: It is forbidden to soak uncooked food in water hot enough that "a hand recoils from it" on the Sabbath.
Practical test: if the heat is so high that a person would avoid drinking it because of it, that is "a hand recoils from it" and forbidden.

paragraphs: "p sheameru rabbotenu za"l (shabbat qmh, b) : en bishshul achar bishshul, mikkol maqom yesh bishshul achar apiyya o tzeliyya; velaken asur latet pat letok maraq o shear mashqeh shehu cham chom shehayyad soledet bo, apillu shehu munnach bikli sheni sheeno omed bikli rishon shehaya al haesh, ella huraq likli sheni; velav davqa pat, ella kol dabar derakeka asur lehannicha betok chammin shehayyad soledet bo. vekatebu happoseqim: meachar dela beqiinan ezeh miqqere rakkik, tzarik lehachmir bekol dabar lebilti yannicho betok chammin shehayyad soledet bo. veotam hammannichin betzalim letok hammaraq, yizzaharu lebilti yenichum beodo cham shehayyad soledet bo, mippene shehem mitmatteqin mechariputam umitbashshelim gam bikli sheni shehayyad soledet bo.

clarification.explanation: The Sages said there is no additional cooking prohibition upon food that has already been cooked ("there is no cooking after cooking"), but there is indeed an additional cooking prohibition upon food that was baked or roasted (and not cooked in water). Therefore it is forbidden to place bread into hot soup or a hot beverage at the heat of "a hand recoils from it," even if the soup is in a "second vessel" (a vessel that did not stand directly on the fire, but into which the dish was transferred from a first vessel). And this law is not specific to bread — any soft item ("rakhikh") is forbidden to place into such a hot liquid. The authorities wrote: since we are not expert in precisely what is considered "soft" and what is not, one should be stringent about everything and not place it into a liquid at the heat of "a hand recoils from it." One who is accustomed to placing onion into soup must be careful not to do so when the soup is too hot, since the onion sweetens (its taste changes) and in effect it cooks even in a hot second vessel.
takeaways: It is forbidden to place bread or any soft item into a hot beverage ("a hand recoils from it") even in a second vessel, out of concern for cooking after baking.
It is advisable to be stringent regarding any soft food item, since it is not always clear what is soft enough to be forbidden.

paragraphs: Hassoker hayyotze min haqqanim hu mebushshal; vekevan deqayma lan, en bishshul achar bishshul - muttar lehannicha hassoker betok hakkeli, ulearot alayv mashqeh cham shehayyad soledet bo; mihu, "chayye-adam" katab sheyyannicha mashqeh hacham techilla letok hakkeli, veaach"k yannicha hassoker betoko; vetob lehizzaher bazeh, deen peseda velo torach bekak.

clarification.explanation: Sugar produced from sugarcane has already undergone a cooking process in its manufacture. Since there is no prohibition of "cooking after cooking," it is permitted to place the sugar in a vessel and pour a hot beverage over it at the heat of "a hand recoils from it." Nevertheless, the author of the "Chayei Adam" wrote that it is more proper to first place the hot beverage in the vessel, and only afterward add the sugar to it — and it is good to be careful in this manner, since there is no loss or effort involved.
takeaways: It is permitted to pour a hot beverage over sugar on the Sabbath, though it is preferable to first pour the beverage and only then add the sugar.

paragraphs: Yesh osin mashqeh qahu meereb-shabbat umannichin al haur kede lishtoto babboqer beyom-shabbat, ak en mannichim betok hakkeli shemmannichin oto al haur "ben" (gargirim) shel qahu harbeh kepi mah shetztzarik, kede shello yihyeh bazeh taam merirut, lekak mannichim "ben" meat, ubabboqer beet sheshshoteh mashqeh zeh mosipin alayv "ben" zeh, veyesh lahem al mah sheyyismoku; ak gam bazeh tob sheyyasimu beshabbat et ha"ben" achar sheyyariqu hammashqeh hannizkar betok hakkos, kede latzet yede choba shear deot; veod, mippene ki haqqahu hi qeluya, veyesh lachush velomar yesh bishshul achar qaleh. veayyen beseper "ginnat-veradim" biklal g', min siman g' ad siman y' mah shekkatab; veayyen "chatam-soper", orach chayyim, siman "d, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: Some are accustomed to prepare coffee ("qahwa") on the eve of the Sabbath and leave it on the fire to drink in the Sabbath morning, but they do not put the full amount of coffee beans needed into the vessel on the fire, so the beverage will not come out too bitter; instead they place a few beans, and in the morning at the time of drinking they add the remaining beans to the cup. They have grounds to rely upon in this, but it is preferable also to add the extra beans only after the beverage has already been poured into the cup — in order to satisfy the other, more stringent opinions as well, and also because there is an additional concern of "cooking after roasting" (since coffee beans are roasted).
takeaways: When preparing coffee on the Sabbath from beans prepared in advance, it is preferable to add the beans into the cup after pouring, rather than directly into the hot vessel.

paragraphs: Keli rishon shehu keli shennishtammesh bo al-gabbe haesh, apillu leachar shehesiro meal haesh, mebashshel kol zeman shehayyad soledet bo, lepikak asur litten tablin letoko; veken hu haddin deasur litten tablin baqqeara ulearot aleha mikkeli rishon shehayyad soledet bo, mippene shehaeruy mebashshel kede qelipa kemo keli rishon; abal muttar litten tablin betok hammaraq shebbaqqeara shehi keli sheni, apillu shehammaraq cham shehayyad soledet bo, mippene shehattablin qashim hem veen lehachmir bahem bikli sheni. v"p sheamarnu sheen issur litten tablin bikli rishon ella davqa beheka shehayyad soledet bo, mikkol maqom tob lizzaher apillu im en hayyad soledet bo, kevan shehu keli rishon - kede laasot harchaqa useyag laddabar; veayyen acharonim za"l.

clarification.explanation: A "first vessel" is a vessel that was used directly on the fire; even after being removed from the fire, it continues "cooking" as long as it retains heat of "a hand recoils from it." Therefore it is forbidden to place spices into it. Likewise it is forbidden to place spices in a bowl and then pour onto them from a hot first vessel, since the pouring (transfer) cooks to the same degree as the first vessel itself. But it is permitted to place spices into soup that is already in a bowl (which is a second vessel), even if the soup is very hot, since spices are hard and one need not be stringent about them in a second vessel. Although the leniency in a first vessel is limited to a case where it no longer has "a hand recoils from it," it is good to be careful even then and not place spices in a first vessel at all, in order to create a safeguard for the matter.
takeaways: Spices should not be placed in a hot first vessel or have a first-vessel pour poured onto them.
It is permitted to season soup in a second vessel (bowl) even if hot, since hard spices do not cook easily.

paragraphs: Hammelach muttar lehannicho bikli rishon achar sheheebiro meal haesh, apillu odennu cham shehayyad soledet bo, musham ditzrika milcha bishshula kebisra detora, vezehu daat mera"n za"l beshulchan aruk; ak harama" za"l behaggahat hashshulchan machmir bemelach apillu bikli sheni shehayyad soledet bo, vetob lehizzaher bazeh, dekamma poseqim chashu lazeh. mikkol maqom im abar venatan melach apillu bikli rishon beodo al haesh, daabad issura lekulle alema - hammaakol muttar, dehammelach batel legabbe hammaakol.

clarification.explanation: Salt may be placed in a first vessel even after it has been removed from the fire, even while it still has heat of "a hand recoils from it," since salt requires strong cooking "like the meat of an ox" (that is, it is difficult to cook) — so ruled Maran in the Shulchan Aruch. But the Rema is stringent and writes that one should be careful with salt even in a hot second vessel, and it is good to be stringent in this manner since many authorities were concerned about it. Nevertheless, if after the fact a person already placed salt even in a first vessel while it was still on the fire (which is a prohibition agreed upon by all), the food itself remains permitted, since the salt is nullified and considered a nullified part of the food.
takeaways: In practice it is good to be stringent and not place salt in a hot vessel, even a second vessel, although by strict law it is permitted in a first vessel.
If after the fact salt was already placed on the fire, the food itself remains permitted.

paragraphs: Muttar latet mayim chammin letok tzonen, vaapillu min keli rishon muttar learot letok mayim tzonen, detachton gober al haelyon umetzanneno; abal asur learot mayim tzonenin letok chammin shebbikli rishon, yaan ki hattachton shehu chammin gober umechammemo, abal im hachammin hem bikli sheni, apillu hayyad soledet bahem muttar learot letokan tzonen. veyesh mattirin gam bikli rishon im noten harbeh mayim tzonenin letok hachammin, dehaynu shehem rabbim yoter al hachammin beopen shello yehe beepshar sheyyitbashshelu, ella raq tapug tzinnatan, dekevan dehatztzonenin merubbin umitarebim tekep mebattel chamimut hachammin. umihu, kol zeh eno ella davqa beshopek hatztzonenin bishpika gedola hakkol bepaam achat letok hachammin, abal meat meat asur learot, shehare mebashshel tekep, umah yoil mah shemmetzannenam aach"k? vekannizkar b"chayye-adam", kelal b', seip g', yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to pour hot water into cold water, and even from a first vessel it is permitted to pour into cold water, since the lower liquid (the cold) "overpowers" the upper one (the hot) and cools it. But it is forbidden to pour cold water into hot water that is in a first vessel, since here the lower one (the hot) overpowers and heats the cold one — and this is considered cooking. If the hot liquid is in a second vessel, it is permitted to pour cold water into it even if it is very hot. Some permit pouring cold water even into a first vessel if the quantity of cold water is very large relative to the hot, such that there is no possibility it will cook but only that its chill will be dispelled. But this leniency applies specifically when the cold water is poured all at once and in a large quantity; if poured little by little, it is forbidden, since each drop is instantly cooked before the overall cooling effect takes hold.
takeaways: Cold water into hot water in a first vessel is forbidden, unless a large quantity is poured all at once, nullifying any possibility of cooking.
Hot into cold is always permitted; pouring cold into a second vessel (even hot) is always permitted.

paragraphs: Muttar litten qiton shel mayim o shear mashqin keneged hammedura lehapig tzinnatan, ubilbad sheyyittenem rachoq mehaesh sheen yekolim lehitchammem beoto maqom ad shettehe hayyad soledet bahem ap im yishheh sham zeman merubbeh, abal asur leyittenem samuk bemaqom sheepshar sheyyitchammemu chom shehayyad soledet bahem, "p sheatta eno mannicham ella raq shaa muetet shettapig tzinnatan bilbad gezera shemma yishkachem veyishhu sham ad sheyyechammu chom shehayyad soledet bo. veinyanim ellu tzerikin hassaara bedaat vehassekel, velo yukal kol ish tam upeti lismok al dato behassearot ellu laasot maaseh.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to place a jug of water or another beverage near a bonfire so that its chill is dispelled, provided the location is far enough from the fire that it cannot possibly heat up to "a hand recoils from it" even if one forgets and leaves it there a long time. But it is forbidden to place it close, where it could heat up to that degree, even if one intends to leave it only briefly, out of concern that one might forget and leave it there until it actually heats up. These matters require judgment and understanding, and an ordinary person cannot rely on his own personal assessment in such cases.
takeaways: A beverage may be cooled near a fire only if its location is far enough that there is no chance it will reach "a hand recoils from it" heat, even if forgotten there.

paragraphs: Hakkobesh kebashin, asur mishshum mebashshel, vegam yesh bazeh issur meabbed; velaken, kol dabar shergilin laasot mimmennu kebashin kegon qishshuin v"nome" (limon matoq) chimmutz vekayyotze, asur limloach ulehannicha lepanayv "p sherotzeh leakelam beotah seuda; abal metabbel min hachatikot achat achat veokel miyyad, velo yitbol shenayim o yoter veyannicha lepanayv. velav davqa dabar shergilin laasot mimmennu kebashin hu deasur, ella kol dabar shehammelach moil leshannot tibo lehapig chariputo kegon tzenon ubatzal veshum vekayyotze middebarim hacharipim, o lematteq chamitzuto, gam ken asur limloach ulehannicha lepanayv, ella metabbel achat achat veokel miyyad, vekannizkar bapposeqim za"l.

clarification.explanation: One who pickles vegetables (soaking in salt or vinegar for long-term preservation) on the Sabbath transgresses both the prohibition of "cooking" and the prohibition of "tanning/processing." Therefore items that are commonly made into pickles, such as squash and sweet-sour lemon, may not be salted and set aside even if one intends to eat them at that very meal. But it is permitted to dip a single piece in salt and eat it immediately, repeatedly — but not to dip several pieces and set them aside before him. This rule is not limited only to items commonly pickled, but any item whose nature the salt changes — such as dispelling its sharpness (radish, onion, garlic) or sweetening its sourness — is likewise forbidden to salt and set aside; rather one must dip one piece at a time and eat immediately.
takeaways: It is forbidden to salt and set aside in advance items whose taste or sharpness the salt changes; only dipping a single piece and eating it immediately, repeatedly, is permitted.

paragraphs: Poh irenu darkam lehabi al hashshulchan qeara melea gargere rimmonim shehem chamutzim, umannichim alehem melach lemateqam mechamitzutam, tzerikin lehizzaher shello yaasu ken beshabbat, v"g deen osin meellu kebashin - kebar katabnu dekol dabar shehammelach moil letaqqeno, asur limloach ulehannicha lepanayv, ella metabbel achat achat veokel miyyad, vehu haddin haka; mihu, im yirtzeh liqqach chatikat rimmon sheyyesh bah kamma gargirim ulehannicha aleha melach uleakelah kullah miyyad, shari, upashut.

clarification.explanation: In Rabbi Yosef Chaim's community it was customary to bring to the table a bowl of sour pomegranate seeds and sprinkle salt over them to sweeten their sourness. One must be careful not to do this on the Sabbath, even though these seeds are not actually made into pickles — for as written, any item whose taste the salt corrects is forbidden to salt and set before a person, but rather one must dip one at a time and eat immediately. But if one wishes to take a whole piece of pomegranate (with several seeds inside it) and salt the whole piece and eat it all at once immediately, this is permitted.
takeaways: Sour pomegranate seeds: one may not salt a quantity and set it aside, but one may salt and eat an entire piece at once immediately.

paragraphs: Kol zeh eno ella beheka dehammelach moil leoto dabar hannimlach leshannot tibo - hen lehapig meriruto, hen lehapig chamitzuto velaken, "p sheen derek likbosh oto dabar, amerinan deasur limloach ulehannicha, abal dabar sheen derek laasot mimmennu kebashin, vegam en hammelach meshanneh tibo, muttar limloach ulehannicha lepanayv; velaken betzim muttar limloach ulehannicha lepanayv, mippene dehabbetzim en derek laasot mehen kebashin, vegam en hammelach meshanneh tibam, ella raq noten bahem taam qetzat; veken hu haddin im shakechu meereb shabbat litten melach battabshil, muttar litten hammelach biqara achar shennitztannen meat sheen hayyad soledet bo, deaz en chashash bishshul bazeh apillu ledaat harama" za"l shekkatabnu leel (halaka y). veha dekatabnu leel deshare bebetzim vetabshil limloach ulehannicha lepanayv, haynu davqa leekol beotah seuda, abal leekol lisuda acheret apillu sheokelah bo bayyom, asur, ukemo shekkatebu rob happoseqim za"l; "g deharab "eliyya raba mattir bazeh, mihu uledaat ha"ture-zahab" za"l besop seip qatan Adonai - im yesh ezeh tzad lomar detob lo sheyyimlach akshav mimmah sheyyimlach aach"k, kegon sheatta hu qetzat cham viqabbel hammelach tepe, en leesor, yeuyyan sham. veen lismok al zeh ella letzorek gadol ukemo shekkatab haggaon rabbenu zalman za"l.

clarification.explanation: The entire prohibition of salting and setting aside applies only when the salt truly changes the food's nature — dispelling bitterness or sourness. But an item that is not commonly made into pickles, and whose nature the salt does not change (only adding a slight taste), may be salted and set before a person in advance. Therefore eggs may be salted and set aside, since eggs are not made into pickles and the salt only gives them taste. Likewise, if one forgot to add salt to a dish before the Sabbath, it is permitted to add salt in the bowl after the dish has cooled somewhat (so that it no longer has "a hand recoils from it"), since then there is no concern of cooking even according to the stringent opinions mentioned earlier. But this entire leniency regarding salt on eggs and cooked dishes applies specifically to eating at that very meal, and not for a different meal even on the same day, as most authorities wrote (there is a minority lenient opinion, but one should not rely on it except in great need).
takeaways: Eggs, and a cooled dish, may be salted, but only for eating at that same meal, not for a later meal.

paragraphs: Lav davqa heka dehammelach meshanneh teba haddabar letaqqeno mimmeriruto o mechamitzuto hu deasur, ella hu haddin im metaqqeno lerakkeko o lehaqshoto name asur, ki gam bazeh nimtza meshanneh tibo vedame lekobesh kebashin; velaken, polin vaadashin shennitbashshelu biqlippatan, asur limloach harbeh beyachad ulehannicham lepanayv, dehammelach moil lerakkek haqqoshi sheyyesh bahem mitztzad qelippatam, vegam zeh domeh lekobesh kebashin, veken dame lemebad. veal ken poh irenu, sheddarkan lebashshel polin sheqqorin "baqli" (sheuit) biqlippatan - im shakechu lehannicha melach beet bishshul, asur lehannicha alehem melach biqara ulehannicha lipnehem, veken hu haddin bipri sheqqorin "lubiyya" ubilshon haqqodesh "rubbeya", im lo natenu bahem melach bebishshul, asur lehannicha alehem achar shehinnicham biqara, dekol ellu hammelach moil lerakkek qelippatan, ella metabbel achat achat bemelach veokel. vezeh happeri sheqqorin bearbe "lubbeya" yesh bo issur yoter, mippene ki poh irenu darkan laasot mizzeh kebashin.

clarification.explanation: The prohibition of salting and setting aside is not limited only to a case where the salt corrects bitterness or sourness, but also when the salt changes the food's texture — softening it or hardening it — this too is considered a change of nature similar to pickling. Therefore beans and lentils that were cooked with their peel are forbidden to be salted in a large quantity and set before them, since the salt softens the hard peel, and this also resembles the processing of hide ("tanning"). Likewise green beans ("baqilla") that were customarily cooked with their peel — if one forgot to add salt during cooking, it is forbidden to add salt to them in the bowl and set them before oneself, and the same applies to a bean pod ("lubiyah"/"rubiyah") that was not salted during cooking — in all these cases one must dip one at a time and eat, not set them out with salt. The lubiyah is even more severe, since in Rabbi Yosef Chaim's community it was customary to actually make pickles from it.
takeaways: Salt that softens a hard peel (beans, lentils, green beans) is likewise forbidden if set out in advance in quantity; only dipping one at a time is permitted.

paragraphs: Haosin "slt" miqqishshuin vekayyotze, dechotekin otam lachatikot qetannot venotenin alehem melach, asur lehamtin alehem ad sheyyeqabbelu taam hammelach veyazziu kede lasim alehem hachometz, ella yizzaher lasim alehem hachometz tekep umiyyad achar netinat hammelach, velo yishheh otam bemelach lebaddo.

clarification.explanation: One who makes a salad ("salata") from squash or similar vegetables by cutting them into small pieces and adding salt, may not wait with the salt alone until the vegetables absorb the taste and "sweat" (release liquids) before adding the vinegar to them — rather one must add the vinegar immediately after the salt, and not let them sit with salt alone.
takeaways: When preparing a salad on the Sabbath, the vinegar must be added immediately after the salt, and the vegetables must not be left in salt alone.

paragraphs: Ha"salta" sheosin miqqishshuin vekol yaraq chay, asur lehannicham betok chometz chazaq keshiur sheyyitten al haur veyarticha, dehave kabush apillu keshiur zeh im hachometz chazaq, ukemo shekkatab haggaon mishbetzot zahab za"l besiman shk", seip qatan g'. veayyen beshulchan aruk yoreh dea, siman q"h, seip b; veayyen "peri-toar" usheare acharonim sham; veayyen "bae-chayye", yoreh dea, siman qs"h, vmg", siman tm"z, v"chuqqot- happesach" sham. umah shekkatab harab "eshel-abraham" besiman shk" bedaat hmg" - en debarayv mukrachim; vaapillu lepi debarayv, la qaamar ella ledaat mg", ak leinyan dina lo chazar middebarayv shekkatab bemishbetzot zahab leesor bipshitut, vezeh barur.

clarification.explanation: A salad of squash or other raw vegetables may not be placed into strong vinegar of such quantity and potency that, had it been placed on fire, it would reach a boil — since this is considered full-fledged "pickling" even if a long time has not yet passed, since strong vinegar acts quickly like cooking. Rabbi Yosef Chaim rejects a certain lenient interpretation (of Rabbi Eshel Avraham) regarding the view of the Magen Avraham, and rules that one should not rely on it, and the simple halacha is to forbid it.
takeaways: Especially strong vinegar (of a kind that could cause boiling on a fire) may not be used to pickle raw vegetables on the Sabbath even briefly.

paragraphs: Asur laasot me-melach merubbim, o shear mashqim im melach merubbim. vela mibbaya oseh latet letok debarim sheddarkam lekobesham lehitqayyem, sheyyesh bazeh leta demeebed veleta dimbashshel ukemo shekkatabti leel, ella apillu oseh me-melach letabbel bahem pitto velatet letok hattabshil, asur laasot harbeh bebat-achat letzorek tibbul shette seudot, ella oseh meat letzorek seuda achat bilbad; vaapillu letzorek seuda achat eno rashshay ella samuk lisuda, abal lo misseuda lisuda.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to prepare on the Sabbath a large quantity of brine (a strong solution of salt and water) or other beverages with much salt. This is clear when the intent is to pickle items in them for long-term preservation — which involves both the prohibition of "processing" and "cooking." But even if the purpose is only to dip bread in it or add it to a dish, it is forbidden to prepare a large quantity at once for two meals — only a small amount for a single meal. And even for a single meal, the brine may be prepared only close to the meal itself, not in advance between one meal and another.
takeaways: Preparing brine on the Sabbath is permitted only in a small quantity, for an immediate meal alone, not in advance and not in a large quantity.

paragraphs: Asur lishpok beshabbat yayin o shear mashqin letok keli sheyyesh bo chometz kede sheggam zeh yihyeh chometz aach"k, dehave kobesh kebashim bekak; veod yesh issur acher - dahare nimtza mekin lachul. velaken lo yashliku temarim hamtullaim letok chabit shel chometz beshabbat, velo tzimmuqim hashsheruyan bemayim letzorek haqqiddush letok chabit shel chometz beshabbat.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to pour wine or another beverage on the Sabbath into a vessel containing vinegar, with the intent that this beverage too will later turn into vinegar — since this is considered "pickling" (an act that introduces something into a preservation/souring process). There is also an additional prohibition involved: preparing on the Sabbath for the sake of a weekday ("preparing from Sabbath for weekday"). Therefore it is forbidden to throw worm-infested dates into a barrel of vinegar on the Sabbath (in order to destroy the worms via the vinegar), and it is likewise forbidden to throw raisins that were soaked in water for Kiddush into a barrel of vinegar on the Sabbath.
takeaways: It is forbidden to add wine, a beverage, dates, or raisins into a barrel of vinegar on the Sabbath, since this is considered forbidden pickling and preparing from one day for another.
